intro.title: Arrays: lists of values
intro.bodyMarkdown:
An **array** is a list of values in one variable, written in square brackets with commas between them. It keeps its values in order.

```
const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
const scores = [72, 88, 95]
console.log(fruits)
console.log(scores.length)
```

Like the characters of a string, each item has an **index** starting at 0: `fruits[0]` is `"apple"`, `fruits[2]` is `"cherry"`. `length` is how many items there are, so the last one is `fruits[fruits.length - 1]`, or `fruits.at(-1)`. An index past the end gives `undefined`.

An array can hold any values, even a mix: `["Sam", 12, true]`. Usually though, one array holds one kind of thing: all names, or all scores. An empty array is `[]`.

`console.log` shows an array with brackets and quotes around the text, like `[ 'apple', 'banana' ]`, so you can see exactly what is in it.

An index can be any expression that gives a number: `scores[i]`, `scores[scores.length - 1]`, `fruits[Math.floor(fruits.length / 2)]`. Together with a `for` loop over the indexes, that lets you visit every item:

```
const scores = [72, 88, 95]
for (let i = 0; i < scores.length; i++) {
  console.log(`Score ${i + 1}: ${scores[i]}`)
}
```

intro.title: Adding and removing items
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Unlike strings, arrays can be changed in place. Four methods add and remove items at the ends:

- `push(x)` adds to the end, and `pop()` removes the last item and gives it back;
- `unshift(x)` adds to the start, and `shift()` removes the first item and gives it back.

```
const queue = ["Ana", "Ben"]
queue.push("Cal")
queue.unshift("Zoe")
console.log(queue)
const served = queue.shift()
console.log(served, queue)
```

You can also set an item by its index: `queue[1] = "Bo"` replaces the second item.

A `const` array can still change. `const` only means the variable always holds the **same array**; what is inside it can change. `queue = []` (a different array) is the thing `const` stops.

A loop with `push` builds a new array from scratch, a pattern you will use constantly: start with `[]`, and push each result.

```
const squares = []
for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
  squares.push(i * i)
}
console.log(squares)
```

intro.title: slice and splice
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Two methods with similar names do very different things.

`slice(start, end)` **copies** part of an array into a new one, from `start` up to (not including) `end`, exactly like a string's `slice`. The original isn't touched. With no arguments, `slice()` copies the whole array.

```
const letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
console.log(letters.slice(1, 3), letters.slice(-2))
console.log(letters)
```

`splice(start, count, ...items)` **changes** the array: it removes `count` items from `start`, puts any `items` in their place, and gives back what it removed.

```
const team = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cal", "Dev"]
const out = team.splice(1, 2)
console.log(out, team)
team.splice(1, 0, "Eli")
console.log(team)
```

A count of 0 removes nothing, so `splice(i, 0, x)` **inserts** `x` at index `i`. `splice(i, 1, x)` replaces one item.

A memory trick: `slice` is a careful knife that takes a copy; `splice` cuts the array itself. When you need the original later, use `slice`.

intro.title: Searching and joining
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Arrays share some methods with strings. `includes(x)` says whether `x` is in the array, and `indexOf(x)` gives the index of the first `x`, or `-1` when there is none.

```
const guests = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cal"]
console.log(guests.includes("Ben"), guests.includes("Dev"))
console.log(guests.indexOf("Cal"), guests.indexOf("Dev"))
```

Both compare with `===`, so the type matters: `[1, 2, 3].includes("2")` is `false`.

`join(separator)` makes one string from all the items, with the separator between them: `["a", "b", "c"].join(", ")` is `"a, b, c"`. The opposite is a string's `split(separator)`, which cuts text into an array: `"a,b,c".split(",")` is `["a", "b", "c"]`.

```
const words = "the quick brown fox".split(" ")
console.log(words, words.length)
console.log(words.join("-"))
```

`reverse()` turns an array around **in place** (it changes the array). `split`, `reverse` and `join` together reverse a sentence's words.

`indexOf` with `splice` removes an item by its value: find where it is, then cut it out, checking for `-1` first.

intro.title: for…of: loop over every item
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Looping over indexes works, but most of the time you want the items, not their positions. `for…of` gives you each item in turn:

```
const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
for (const fruit of fruits) {
  console.log(fruit.toUpperCase())
}
```

Read it as "for each fruit of fruits". The variable (`fruit`) is a new `const` on each run, so pick a name that says what one item is: `for (const score of scores)`, `for (const name of names)`.

All the loop patterns still work: a running total, a count, the biggest so far, and building a new array with `push`, only shorter:

```
const scores = [72, 88, 95, 61]
let total = 0
const high = []
for (const score of scores) {
  total += score
  if (score >= 80) high.push(score)
}
console.log(total, high)
```

`for…of` works on strings too, one character at a time: `for (const ch of "hello")`.

When you do need the index as well, use `entries()`: `for (const [i, fruit] of fruits.entries())` gives both (the square brackets are explained in the destructuring stage). Or use a classic `for` loop.

`break` and `continue` work in `for…of` just as in other loops.

intro.title: Objects: named values
intro.bodyMarkdown:
An array keeps values in order by number. An **object** keeps values by **name**. It is written in curly braces, as `key: value` pairs separated by commas:

```
const pet = { name: "Rex", species: "dog", age: 4 }
console.log(pet.name, pet.age)
console.log(pet)
```

Each key is a **property**. Read one with a dot, `pet.name`, or with square brackets and the key as text, `pet["name"]`. Brackets are needed when the key is in a variable: `const field = "age"; pet[field]`. A property that isn't there gives `undefined`.

Properties can be changed, added and removed, even on a `const` object (as with arrays, `const` only fixes which object it is):

```
const pet = { name: "Rex", age: 4 }
pet.age = 5
pet.owner = "Sam"
delete pet.name
console.log(pet)
```

`"key" in object` checks whether a property exists. `Object.keys(obj)` gives an array of the keys, `Object.values(obj)` the values, and `Object.entries(obj)` `[key, value]` pairs, which a `for…of` can loop over.

```
const stock = { apples: 12, pears: 0, plums: 7 }
for (const [fruit, count] of Object.entries(stock)) {
  console.log(`${fruit}: ${count}`)
}
```

When a variable has the same name as the key, there is a shortcut: `{ name, age }` means `{ name: name, age: age }`.

intro.title: Nested data
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Real data mixes the two. A class is an **array of objects**, one per student; a student is an **object with an array** of scores. Values can be nested as deep as needed.

```
const students = [
  { name: "Ana", scores: [90, 85] },
  { name: "Ben", scores: [72, 64] },
]
console.log(students[1].name)
console.log(students[0].scores[1])
```

Read the path one step at a time: `students[0]` is Ana's object, `.scores` is her array, `[1]` is its second item. (The comma after the last item is allowed, and makes adding another line easier.)

Looping over an array of objects is the everyday case: `for (const s of students)` gives each object, and `s.name` reads from it.

```
const cart = [
  { item: "pen", price: 1.5, qty: 4 },
  { item: "pad", price: 3, qty: 2 },
]
let total = 0
for (const line of cart) {
  total += line.price * line.qty
}
console.log(total)
```

If something along the path might be missing, `?.` stops safely and gives `undefined` instead of an error: `user.address?.city`.

`JSON.stringify(data)` turns nested data into text, and `JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)` lays it out over several lines, which makes it easy to read. (You will meet JSON properly in quest 9.)

intro.title: Destructuring
intro.bodyMarkdown:
**Destructuring** unpacks values from an array or an object into variables in one line.

From an object, name the properties you want in curly braces; each becomes a variable of the same name:

```
const pet = { name: "Rex", species: "dog", age: 4 }
const { name, age } = pet
console.log(name, age)
```

Rename with a colon (`const { name: petName } = pet`), and give a default with `=` for a property that may be missing (`const { owner = "nobody" } = pet`).

From an array, use square brackets: the variables are filled in order. Skip an item with an empty place between commas.

```
const podium = ["Mia", "Jo", "Kai"]
const [gold, silver] = podium
const [, , bronze] = podium
console.log(gold, silver, bronze)
```

Array destructuring gives a neat swap, with no spare variable: `[a, b] = [b, a]`. One catch when you leave out semicolons: a line that **starts** with `[` is read as part of the line before it. Start such a line with a semicolon: `;[a, b] = [b, a]`.

You have already used it: `for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(obj))` destructures each `[key, value]` pair as the loop gets it. It works in the loop variable of a `for…of` over objects too: `for (const { name, age } of people)`.

intro.title: Spread and rest: ...
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Three dots, `...`, do two jobs. Where values are expected, **spread** opens an array (or object) up into its items. Where a variable is expected, **rest** collects items into one.

Spread copies and combines arrays without changing the originals:

```
const a = [1, 2]
const b = [3, 4]
const both = [...a, ...b]
const copy = [...a]
const more = [0, ...a, 99]
console.log(both, copy, more)
```

It works for objects too. Later properties win, which makes "a copy with some changes" easy:

```
const base = { size: "M", colour: "blue" }
const custom = { ...base, colour: "red" }
console.log(custom, base)
```

Spread also passes an array's items to something that wants separate values: `Math.max(...scores)`.

Rest is the other way round: in destructuring, `const [first, ...others] = list` puts everything after the first item into `others`, and `const { password, ...safe } = user` gives an object of all the other properties.

These are **shallow** copies: nested arrays and objects inside are shared, not copied. For flat data, that is all you need.

intro.title: Map and Set
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Two more collections fill gaps that arrays and objects leave.

A **Set** holds values with no repeats: adding something it already has does nothing. It is the quickest way to remove duplicates and to ask "have I seen this?".

```
const seen = new Set()
seen.add("red")
seen.add("blue")
seen.add("red")
console.log(seen.size, seen.has("blue"))
console.log([...new Set([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])])
```

`add`, `has`, `delete` and `size` are its main parts. `[...set]` turns it back into an array, and `for…of` loops over it in the order things were added.

A **Map** holds key-value pairs, like an object, but it is built for lookups that change a lot: `set(key, value)`, `get(key)`, `has(key)`, `delete(key)` and `size`. Its keys can be anything, even numbers or objects, and they keep the order they were added.

```
const stock = new Map()
stock.set("apples", 12)
stock.set("pears", 3)
stock.set("apples", stock.get("apples") - 2)
console.log(stock.get("apples"), stock.size)
for (const [fruit, count] of stock) {
  console.log(fruit, count)
}
```

Counting is a Map's classic job: for each item, `counts.set(item, (counts.get(item) ?? 0) + 1)`. `get` gives `undefined` for a key it hasn't seen, and `?? 0` turns that into 0.

As a rule of thumb: an object for a thing with fixed properties (a user, a book); a Map for a lookup table that grows; a Set for "unique items".
